summary:
Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu stands under India's national framework. India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, which replaces the 2019 law's self-identification route with recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex persons, and requires medical certification for identity recognition. The amendment reverses the self-identification principle set by the Supreme Court's 2014 ruling in the National Legal Services Authority case.

Recognition now rests on documents a visitor may have to obtain or renew. Medical boards and district authorities must certify gender-affirming surgery, and passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination, a requirement the Allahabad High Court addressed when it granted relief in February 2026. The 2019 law's original self-identification route, which a trans traveller would previously have relied on, no longer governs.

The narrowed categories exclude many trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside them, as rights activists including Akkai Padmashali have stated, describing the amendment as an attack on the right to exist. The government presents the narrower definition as targeting welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection.

The amendment adds offences including up to life imprisonment for coercing or alluring anyone to be transgender. Human Rights Watch warned in its report of 26 March 2026 that this provision could criminalise support networks, creating exposure for a visitor who contacts advocacy or peer groups. Presidential assent was pending in late March 2026, and a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel asked the government to withdraw the bill, calling the removal of self-identification a setback against the 2014 ruling.

The wider entry and stay baseline is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender, and trans people arrested by that force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, Central Industrial Security Force personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification.

The high courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

No deviation from the national position is documented for Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu: the recognition scheme, checkpoint practices and court protections described here apply as national law and national enforcement.
tangentialFactors:
Census-recorded transgender persons number 487,803, of whom only about 32,500 hold identity cards, while the estimated national transgender population is around two million. The gap between census count and estimate indicates that most trans people in India, visitors included, hold no government identity document recording their gender.

The March 2026 amendment is a change in the direction of restriction rather than expansion: it narrows a 2019 statute that itself followed the expansive 2014 Supreme Court recognition, and it narrows protections that were already eroded in 2024 when the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita replaced the Indian Penal Code.

Official and critical readings of the amendment diverge on purpose rather than on text. The government frames the narrower definition as a way to target welfare benefits and anti-trafficking protection; critics, including a Supreme Court-appointed advisory panel, treat the removal of self-identification as a setback and urge withdrawal of the bill.

Assessment elsewhere in the country is comparatively restrained on policing. The UK Home Office country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, which sits alongside the specific checkpoint incidents documented in 2024 and 2026.
localsOnly:
For residents, legal identity now depends on certification rather than declaration. Medical boards and district authorities certify gender-affirming surgery before identity documents are issued, and only about 32,500 of the 487,803 census-recorded transgender people nationally hold identity cards, so the certification route has been taken up by a small fraction of the population.

Resident advocacy carries a specific criminal risk under the amendment's coercion and allurement offence, which carries up to life imprisonment and which Human Rights Watch warns could criminalise support networks, including peer groups, counsellors and family members who assist someone in transition.

The welfare and anti-trafficking framing of the amendment has practical consequences for residents, since the narrower definition governs eligibility for welfare schemes, while the government presents the change as widening access to those schemes for those it recognises.

Protection machinery for residents runs through the high courts. The Madras High Court's 7 June 2021 guidelines in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police bind police on sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy, and direct the National Medical Commission and education authorities, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita in force since 2024 no longer carries the gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that the Indian Penal Code provided.

Same-sex couples have been acknowledged by courts as family units, but same-sex marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable to residents.
outOfScopeNotes:
Presidential assent to the March 2026 amendment was pending as of late March 2026; whether it has since been granted, and the date of assent, is not sourced in the inventory.

Whether Dādra and Nagar Haveli and Damān and Diu has issued any local implementing rules, forms or medical-board procedures under the amended Act is not sourced, nor is any union-territory police instruction on gender-verification encounters.

The inventory does not record incidents involving trans travellers specific to this union territory; the checkpoint cases cited are from other parts of the country and are used to illustrate national enforcement practice.

The number of census-recorded transgender persons resident in this union territory, and local identity-card issuance figures, are not sourced.

Whether the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita contains any replacement provision addressing sexual violence against transgender people is not resolved in the inventory, which records only the removal of the gender-identity-specific offences.
